text.p: Administrators for bankrupt Dutch plane-maker Fokker said on Wednesday that a fire-sale of remaining assets now looked inevitable after the Malaysian government confirmed it had pulled out of rescue talks.
"We are afraid the only option will be to proceed with our plans to dispose of the company's assets," said Ben Knueppe, spokesman for Fokker's court-appointed receivers.
Official word from the Dutch government on the fate of one of Europe's aviation pioneers is still awaited.
But the decision by the Malaysian government -- touted as Fokker's final lifeline -- almost certainly brings the curtain down on more than 75 years of aircraft manufacturing in the Netherlands.
"We entered into serious negotiations but I don't think we can proceed any longer," Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told journalists in Kuala Lumpur earlier on Wednesday.

Malaysia's Ministry of Finance Secretary-General Clifford Herbert added that the problem had been over funds which Dutch counterparties in the talks wanted the government to put on the table before allowing it to look at its books.
"Without due diligence, we cannot make a financial commitment," he said, referring to the usual thorough audit potential investors carry out on a target company.
But Knueppe said the initial sum asked of the Malaysian government was small and that the problem was more one of commitment to a deal he recognised as facing huge hurdles.
"The Malaysians never showed they were really in love with Fokker, at least as much as the Dutch parties, and given the time constraints, that is what was needed," he said.
"It was a tough project and would have only been possible with highly motivated candidates," Knueppe added.
Dutch engineering group Stork, which bought the profitable aircraft maintenance and components units, and industrial investment group Deleye had been ready to help Fokker to avoid collapse.

Fokker's administrators announced on Tuesday that Stork had informed them of the decision by Malaysia's state investment arm Khazanah Nasional Berhad. This was not to put any money on the table and had prompted Stork's withdrawal from the resurrection talks.
The Dutch government and the receivers have fought for a year to keep Fokker airborne after principal shareholder Daimler Benz cut off vital cash support in March 1996.

The move plunged Fokker into bankruptcy and caused 5,600 job losses in the biggest single lay-off in Dutch history. Its payroll, which three years ago topped 13,000, has dwindled to a handful putting the finishing touches on the last three Fokker aircraft under production.
Anxious to preserve the flagship firm in any form possible, the Dutch government embarked on a frantic international search for potential partners.

Canadian and Russian firms entered, and exited, the ring but one potential saviour that seemed more serious than the others was South Korea's Samsung Aerospace. It was assembling a regional consortium with ambitions to build a new generation of small jet planes in the Far East.
But after months of talks and shuttling of delegations between Amsterdam and Seoul, Samsung and its partners decided the risks outweighed the potential rewards.
The story took a bizarre twist last month when Saudi Arabia's billionaire Prince al-Waleed, nephew to King Fahd, was touted as interested in buying into the company.

But like so many other Fokker rumours, that too came to nothing and a week after the possibility surfaced the prince bought a five percent stake in Trans World Airlines Inc, the world's seventh largest air carrier.

Around the same time, the Malaysian government was expressing growing interest in Fokker and there was a glimmer of hope when a delegation from Khazanah arrived in the Netherlands last month to view Fokker's assembly facilities and to examine its books.
That too has now faded and the company's high-tech factories on the outskirts of Amsterdam must now wait to be carved up and sold to the highest bidder.
Knueppe said preparations for the asset sale would be lengthy and postpone Fokker's extinction until well beyond the summer.
